newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Uzbek leader warns of Taleban advance in spring.
newsitem.headline: Uzbek leader warns of Taleban advance in spring.

text.p: Uzbek President Islam Karimov said on Friday that a possible advance by Afghanistan's radical Islamic Taleban militia to the borders of former Soviet Central Asia would destabilise the tense region.

"It is hard to imagine the consequences if the Taleban reach the banks of the Amu Darya," said Karimov, referring to the river that forms part of the border between Afghanistan and the Central Asian states of Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan.

"Such a danger exists and we have discussed possible measures to be taken in case of an eventual escalation of tension and a Taleban move towards the southern border of the commonwealth (CIS)," Karimov told a news conference following a five-nation summit in the Kazakh capital Almaty.
He gave no details of the measures discussed at the summit, held to discuss a regional environmental catastrophe caused by the shrinking of the Aral Sea.

But Karimov said the Central Asian leaders expected the Taleban, which captured the Afghan capital Kabul last September, to try and wrest control of northern Afghanistan from rival warlords this spring.
Russia and the Central Asian states fear the Taleban's radical brand of Islam and fighting close to their borders could destabilise their own hard-hit region.
Keeping fundamental Islamists at bay was one of the main aims of the 1979-1989 Soviet occupation of Afghanistan.
Earlier this week, defence ministers from Russia, Uzbekistan and two other Central Asian states met in Tashkent to work out ways of holding the Taleban back from the north.
Western aid agencies based in Central Asia are also preparing for a Taleban advance this spring.

"We're not expecting a huge influx of refugees," said one aid worker. "We'd be more worried if Afghan commanders come over the border seeking a safe haven, which could be very disruptive in a place like Tajikistan," he added.
